opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it matters a lot, and for a few different reasons.

The first is just scientific: these systems are still very early. When we released the AI Scientist, it was clear it could produce papers that looked plausible and occasionally had interesting ideas, but it also made mistakes, it hallucinated results sometimes, and its sense of what's actually novel was pretty shaky. If you keep that behind closed doors, you're the only one who gets to find those failure modes. Opening it up means hundreds of researchers start poking at it, finding where it breaks, building better reviewers and verification steps. That's how the whole field moves faster.

With Shinka in particular, part of the motivation was sample efficiency. A lot of the impressive evolutionary code-search results, things like AlphaEvolve, came from setups with enormous compute budgets that most academic labs simply don't have. We wanted to show you can get state-of-the-art-ish results, like on circle packing, with a few hundred program evaluations instead of thousands, and then hand that to people so a PhD student with a modest API budget can actually use it on their own problem. Otherwise "AI-driven discovery" just becomes something only three or four companies can do.

Then there's the community and safety side. If these tools are going to change how research gets done, the community needs to have a say in the norms: how you disclose AI-generated work, how you review it, what sandboxing you need when an agent is executing code it wrote itself. You can't have that conversation in the abstract. People need to run the thing, see where it surprises them, and form their own opinions.

And honestly, open-sourcing it is also a bit of humility. I don't think we have the best ideas about what to point these systems at. Someone working in materials science or in some niche of combinatorics will find applications we'd never think of. The most exciting outcomes probably won't come from us. They'll come from people taking the tool and doing something weird with it.

r001.rationale: The response says open access lets many researchers find failure modes, shape community norms, and discover applications the creators would miss, identifying collective input as a way to shape AI discovery tools.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it matters for a few reasons, and they're not all the obvious ones.

The first is just scientific honesty. If you're going to claim that a system can run the loop of ideation, experimentation, and writing up results, people need to be able to poke at it. When we released the AI Scientist, a big part of what we got back was criticism, and a lot of it was fair. People found that the generated papers had errors, that the experiments were sometimes shallow, that the novelty checks were weak. That's exactly what you want, because the alternative is a demo video and a press release that nobody can verify. The field moves faster when the failure modes are public.

The second reason is that these systems are really workflows, not models. The interesting part of the AI Scientist or ShinkaEvolve is not some proprietary weight file, it's the scaffolding: how you structure the search, how you keep a population of candidate programs, how you decide which ideas to spend compute on, how you let the model propose mutations at the level of code rather than hyperparameters. That kind of thing is best thought of as infrastructure. If it's open, a grad student with a single GPU and an API key can plug in their own domain, their own evaluation function, and find out whether evolutionary search over programs actually helps in their corner of science. We can't do that for them. We don't know all the problems that are worth attacking.

With Shinka specifically, the thing we cared about was sample efficiency. A lot of earlier work in this space, including stuff like AlphaEvolve, needed a huge number of evaluations to get anywhere, which effectively locked it behind large labs. We wanted something where a few hundred samples gets you a competitive solution, because that's the regime most researchers actually live in. If that's true, then keeping it closed would somewhat defeat the point. The whole argument is that this should be accessible.

There's also a more cultural angle. I think there's a real risk that automated discovery becomes something that only three or four companies do behind closed doors, and the rest of the community just consumes the outputs. I find that uncomfortable, partly because science has always been a community activity with peer review and reproducibility baked in, and partly because I don't think the people building these tools should be the only ones deciding what counts as a discovery. When the tools are open, you get people building better evaluators, better novelty checks, better ways to catch the system fooling itself. Those are hard problems and they need many hands.

And finally, honestly, it's just how I like to work. Coming from the academic side, open source was always the default. You put the code out, people break it, you fix it, everyone learns something. I don't see a reason that should change just because the thing being released can itself write papers.

r001.rationale: The response says open tools let the wider community build better evaluators, novelty checks, and safeguards, and argues that many people should help shape what counts as discovery. This clearly presents collective input as a reason for openness.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest reason is that we don’t want the ability to automate scientific discovery to be concentrated in a handful of well-funded labs. If you’re a student with an interesting idea, or a researcher in a smaller group, you should be able to experiment with these systems, understand how they work, and adapt them to your own problems.

And making something like the AI Scientist or Shinka open allows people to interrogate it. Where does it actually help? Where does it fail? Is it producing something novel, or just exploiting a weakness in the evaluation? Those are questions that benefit from lots of people looking at the same system and trying different things.

For me, it’s also about enabling research that we wouldn’t have thought to do ourselves. We can build a tool and demonstrate a few applications, but the community has much more diverse expertise. Giving people the ability to build on it is how you find out what it’s really useful for.

r001.rationale: The response says broad community participation lets people interrogate, experiment with, and build on the tools, drawing on diverse expertise to discover their uses. This communicates collective intelligence shaping their development and future.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that discovery shouldn’t be something that only a handful of very well-resourced labs can participate in. If you make these tools openly available, people can inspect how they work, reproduce the experiments, and adapt them to problems that we might never have thought about.

That’s particularly important with something like the AI Scientist. Producing a scientific-looking result is one thing; establishing that it’s correct and useful is another. You want people to be able to look at the entire process, find the failure modes, and improve the evaluation.

And with Shinka, the exciting part is giving people a way to explore and improve algorithms in their own domains. We’re a small team—we can only try so many things. Opening up the tools allows a much broader community to contribute ideas and discover where these approaches actually help. To me, that collective experimentation is a big part of how the field makes progress.

r001.rationale: The response says open access lets a much broader community contribute ideas, inspect and improve the tools, and collectively experiment—making community input a reason for openness.
